      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Acne</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Pimples</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Zits</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">Acne</span> is a common skin disease that causes pimples. Pimples form when hair follicles 
under your skin clog up. Most pimples form on the face, neck, back, chest, and shoulders. Anyone can get <span class="qt0">acne</span>, but 
it is common in teenagers and young adults. It is not serious, but it can cause scars.</p><p>No one knows exactly what causes <span class="qt0">acne</span>. Hormone changes, such as those during the teenage 
years and pregnancy, probably play a role. There are many myths about what causes <span class="qt0">acne</span>. Chocolate and greasy foods are often 
blamed, but there is little evidence that foods have much effect on <span class="qt0">acne</span> in most people. 
Another common myth is that dirty skin causes <span class="qt0">acne</span>; however, blackheads and pimples are not 
caused by dirt. Stress doesn't cause <span class="qt0">acne</span>, but stress can make it worse.</p><p>If you have <span class="qt0">acne</span>:</p><ul><li>	Clean your skin gently </li><li>	Try not to touch your skin </li><li>	Avoid the sun </li></ul><p>Treatments for <span class="qt0">acne</span> include medicines and creams.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin 
Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hidradenitissuppurativa.html">
      <content name="title">Hidradenitis Suppurativa</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Acne</span> inversa</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Suppurative hidradenitis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is hidradenitis suppurativa (HS)?<p>Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic skin disease. Another name for it is <span class="qt0">acne</span> inversa. It causes painful, boil-like lumps that form under the skin. It often affects areas where the skin rubs together, such as your armpits and groin. The lumps become inflamed and painful. They often break open, causing abscesses that drain fluid and pus. As the abscesses heal, they can cause scarring of the skin.</p>What causes hidradenitis suppurativa (HS)?<p>The lumps in HS form because of blockages of the hair follicles. The blocked hair follicles trap bacteria, which leads to inflammation and rupture. In most cases, the cause of the blockages is unknown. Genetics, environment, and hormonal factors may play a role.</p><p>HS is not caused by bad hygiene, and it cannot be spread to others.</p>Who is more likely to get hidradenitis suppurativa (HS)?<p>HS typically starts after puberty, usually in the teens or twenties. It is more common in:</p><ul><li>Women</li><li>People who are Black</li><li>People with a family history of HS</li><li>People who are overweight or have obesity</li><li>People who smoke</li></ul>What are the symptoms of hidradenitis suppurativa (HS)?<p>The symptoms of HS include:</p><ul><li>Small pitted areas of skin containing blackheads.</li><li>Painful, red, lumps that get bigger and break open. This causes abscesses that drain fluid and pus. They may itch and have an unpleasant odor.</li><li>The abscesses heal very slowly, come back over time, and can lead to scarring and tunnels under the skin.</li></ul><p>Symptoms of HS can range from mild to severe. They can include: </p><ul><li>Only one or a few lumps in one area of the skin.</li><li>Lumps that keep coming back, get bigger, and break open. The lumps form in more than one area of the body.</li><li>Lumps that are widespread, along with scarring, and chronic (long-term) pain that may make it hard to move.</li></ul><p>Because of the difficulty of dealing with the disease, people with HS are at risk for depression and anxiety.</p>How is hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for HS. It can be hard to diagnose in the early stages because it can look like pimples or <span class="qt0">acne</span>. To find out if you have HS, your health care provider:</p><ul><li> Will ask about your medical history and your symptoms</li><li>Will look at the lumps on your skin</li><li>May take a sample of the skin or pus (if there is any) and send it to a lab for testing</li></ul><p>Your provider may refer you to a dermatologist (a doctor who specializes in skin disorders) to get a diagnosis or treatment.</p>What are the treatments for hidradenitis suppurativa?<p>Treatments focus on the symptoms, but they are not always effective for everyone. The treatments depend on how severe the disease is and may include:</p><ul><li>Medicines, including steroids, antibiotics, pain relievers, hormone pills, and medicines that fight inflammation. In mild cases, the medicines may be topical (applied to your skin), injected or taken orally (by mouth).</li><li>Biologics, which are a type of medicine made from living sources, such as cells, tissues, and proteins.</li><li>Procedures or surgery to remove the lumps and scars or make the sores go away.</li><li>Laser hair removal may be helpful in the early stages of HS.</li></ul><p>It may also help if you can avoid things that can irritate your skin, by:</p><ul><li>Wearing loose-fitting clothing</li><li>Staying at a healthy weight</li><li>Quitting smoking</li><li>Avoiding heat and humidity</li><li>Being careful not to injure your skin</li></ul></content>

      <content name="title">Rosacea</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Acne</span> Rosacea</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Rosacea is a long-term disease that affects your skin and sometimes your eyes. It causes redness and pimples. Rosacea is most common in women and people with fair skin. It most often affects middle-aged and older adults.</p><p>In most cases, rosacea only affects the face. Symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Frequent redness of the face, or flushing </li><li>Small, red lines under the skin</li><li><span class="qt0">Acne</span></li><li>A swollen nose</li><li>Thick skin, usually on the forehead, chin, and cheeks </li><li>Red, dry, itchy eyes and sometimes vision problems </li></ul><p>No one knows what causes rosacea. You may be more likely to have it if you blush a lot or if rosacea runs in your family. Rosacea is not dangerous. There is no cure, but treatments can help. They include medicines and sometimes surgery.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/polycysticovarysyndrome.html">
      <content name="title">Polycystic Ovary Syndrome</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">PCOS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Stein-Leventhal Syndrome</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)? <p>Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), also known as polyendocrine metabolic ovary syndrome (PMOS), is the name of a hormonal disorder. PCOS affects the ovaries, as well as many other parts of the body.</p><p>If you have PCOS, you usually have at least two of these problems:</p><ul><li>Not ovulating. Normally, your ovaries make the egg that is released each month as part of a healthy menstrual cycle. This is called ovulation. But with PCOS, the egg may not develop as it should, or it may not be released during ovulation. Your periods may be irregular, or you may not have them at all.</li><li>High levels of androgens. Androgens are hormones that are important for normal male sexual development. Women normally make smaller amounts of androgens. Having higher levels of androgens can cause you to have extra body or facial hair (called hirsutism).</li><li>Growths in one or both ovaries. These growths are often clumps of ovarian follicles that have stopped developing. They may appear as cysts, which are small fluid-filled sacs</li></ul><p>Although it's less common, you may not have growths in your ovaries. You may only have symptoms of PCOS, not ovulate, and have high levels of androgens.</p>What causes polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>The exact cause of PCOS is unknown. Research has shown that different factors may play a role, including:</p><ul><li>Genetics. PCOS tends to run in families.</li><li>Imbalances in androgen levels.</li><li>Insulin resistance. This is a condition in which your body can't use insulin properly. Insulin is a hormone that helps move blood glucose (also called blood sugar) into your cells to give them energy. Insulin resistance can lead to high blood glucose levels.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>PCOS often develops as young as age 11 or 12, around the time of your first period. But you can develop it later.</p><p>The symptoms can vary from person to person. Some women have few or even no symptoms. They may not realize they have PCOS until they have trouble getting pregnant. Other women may have more severe symptoms.</p><p>The symptoms of PCOS may include:</p><ul><li>Irregular or missed menstrual periods.</li><li>Too much hair on the face, chest, stomach, or thighs.</li><li>Obesity, weight gain, or trouble losing weight.</li><li>Severe <span class="qt0">acne</span> which may be hard to treat.</li><li>Oily skin.</li><li>Patches of thickened dark skin (called acanthosis nigricans).</li><li>Infertility. PCOS is one of the most common causes of infertility. But many women with PCOS can still get pregnant.</li></ul>What other health problems are linked to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>PCOS is linked to many other health problems, including:</p><ul><li>Insulin resistance, which can lead to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.</li><li>Heart disease. Having PCOS increases your risk, and this risk goes up as you age.</li><li>High blood pressure.</li><li>High LDL ("bad") cholesterol and low HDL ("good") cholesterol. This increases your risk of heart disease.</li><li>Endometrial hyperplasia, a condition in which the lining of your uterus, or womb, becomes too thick. This can increase your risk for endometrial cancer, also called uterine cancer.</li><li>Sleep apnea, a disorder that causes you to repeatedly stop breathing during sleep.</li><li>Depression and anxiety.</li></ul><p>Although there are links between PCOS and these conditions, researchers do not know whether:</p><ul><li>PCOS causes some of these problems</li><li>Some of these problems cause PCOS, OR</li><li>There are other conditions that cause both PCOS and these other health problems</li></ul><p>Not everyone who has PCOS will have all these problems. However, you and your health care provider may want to monitor your health for signs of them, so they can be treated early.</p>How is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for PCOS. To find out if you have PCOS, your provider: </p><ul><li>Will do a physical exam, which will include looking for the physical signs of PCOS.</li><li>Will ask about your medical history and family health history.</li><li>May do a pelvic exam to check for signs of extra male hormones and to see if your ovaries are enlarged or swollen.</li><li>May order a pelvic ultrasound to look for growths on your ovaries and check the thickness of your endometrium (the lining of your uterus, or womb).</li><li>May order blood tests, including tests to check your hormone levels.</li></ul>What are the treatments for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>Treatments for PCOS can help you manage your symptoms. The treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Lifestyle changes, which can help reduce many symptoms. They can also lower your risk for or help manage related health problems. These changes include:
  <ul><li>Maintaining a healthy weight</li><li>Getting regular physical activity</li><li>Eating healthy foods</li></ul>
</li><li>Medicines:<ul><li>Hormonal birth control, such as pills, shots, and IUDs, can make your period more regular. They may also help remove <span class="qt0">acne</span> and extra facial and body hair. But it's only an option if you're not currently trying to get pregnant.</li><li>Anti-androgen medicines, which block the effect of androgens. This can help reduce hair loss on your head, the growth of facial and body hair, and <span class="qt0">acne</span>. Providers do use them to help with these symptoms, but anti-androgen medicines are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat PCOS. These medicines can cause problems during pregnancy. Your provider may have you take them with birth control (to prevent pregnancy).</li><li>Insulin-sensitizing medicines, which are medicines that are used to treat type 2 diabetes. They improve insulin resistance and keep your blood glucose levels steady. They may also lower your androgen levels. They are not approved by the FDA to treat PCOS. But they may help with your symptoms.</li><li>Medicines for <span class="qt0">acne</span>. These medicines come in pills, creams, or gels.</li></ul></li><li>Treatments for hair removal, such as facial hair removal creams, laser hair removal, and electrolysis.</li><li>Fertility treatments if you are having trouble getting pregnant. They include medicines and procedures such as in vitro fertilization (IVF).</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/scars.html">
      <content name="title">Scars</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cicatrix</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hypertrophic Scar</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Keloids</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Keloid scar</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A scar is a permanent patch of skin that grows over a wound. It forms when your body heals itself after a cut, scrape, burn, or sore. You can also get scars from surgery that cuts through the skin, infections like chickenpox, or skin conditions like <span class="qt0">acne</span>. Scars are often thicker, as well as pinker, redder, or shinier, than the rest of your skin. </p><p>How your scar looks depends on:</p><ul><li>How big and deep your wound is</li><li>Where it is </li><li>How long it takes to heal </li><li>Your age</li><li>Your inherited tendency to scar</li></ul><p>Scars usually fade over time but never go away completely. If the way a scar looks bothers you, various treatments might minimize it. These include surgical revision, dermabrasion, laser treatments, injections, chemical peels, and creams. </p></content>
